rules_text:
Rules summary Contents 1 Gameplay (Four Players) 1.1 Setup 1.2 Deal 1.3 Play 1.4 Scoring 2 Variants 2.1 Bid Whist 2.1.1 Bidding Phase 2.1.2 After Bidding 2.2 Two Player Whist 2.3 Solitaire Mode Gameplay (Four Players) Setup Players are split into teams of 2, with partners sitting across. A standard 52 card deck is used. The cards in each suit rank (from high to low) A > K > Q > ... > 2. Deal The game consists of a series of hands. The turn to deal rotates clockwise with each hand. Deal each player 13 cards, with the dealer's last card turned face up to indicate trumps. The trump suit beats any of the other three suits played in that hand. Play The play begins with the player to the dealer's left, who leads the first card. Play follows clockwise. Each player must follow the suit led, if they can. If not, they may play any other card in their hand. The player who has played the highest trump card, or if no trump was played, the highest card of the suit led, wins the trick. That player then leads to the next trick. Continue until all tricks have been played and won. Scoring When all 13 tricks have been played, the side which won more tricks scores 1 point for each trick they won in excess of 6. Game ends when a team reaches the target score. That team wins. Variants Target Score: 5, 7, or 10 Bid Whist Two jokers are added. Jokers are the highest trump cards, except in no-trump bids where jokers are worthless. With four players, each player is dealt 12 cards, not 13. Bidding Phase Before playing tricks, there is a bidding phase. Clockwise, each player may bid or pass. The dealer is forced to bid if everyone else passes. When bidding, indicate the number of tricks to take (3-7 for 9-13 tricks) and the type (Uptown (A > K > ... 2), Downtown (A > 2 > ... > K), No Trump). Larger numbers are higher than smaller numbers, and No Trump is higher than Uptown/Downtown. The highest bidder becomes the declarer. If they named Uptown or Downtown, they must name the trump suit. Otherwise, they must name if the hand is played Uptown or Downtown. After Bidding The declarer draws 6 cards from the kitty and discards 6 cards, and this counts as a scored trick. Only the declarer side wins or loses points. If they make the bid, they gain the number of points corresponding to their bid. Otherwise, deduct that from the declarer side. Game also ends when a team reaches negative of the target score (e.g. -7 for target score 7). That team loses, and the other team wins. Two Player Whist Each player is dealt 26 cards: 8 straw piles (piles of 2 cards) and a hand of 10 cards. If playing Bid Whist, deal 2 fewer straw piles. If playing Bid Whist, the types of bids become High (win tricks) or Low (avoid tricks). If the non-dealer bids High, they automatically becomes the declarer. The dealer leads the first trick if the non-dealer bids High. Otherwise, the non-dealer leads first. Each trick consists of 4 cards, 2 from each player. Cards can be played from the hand or the top of straw piles. Solitaire Mode For details, go to https://boardgamegeek.com/thread/2969333/whist-solitaire .

---

[Rating: 2/10] AUG/14 - I'm not much for standard-deck card games (Spades and Golf are the only ones I really play), and this one just seems like a more convoluted, less fun version of Spades.

[Rating: 2/10] :thumbsdown: communal cards :thumbsdown: strategically shallow :thumbsdown: tediously tactical

[Rating: 3/10] A fine choice to play if all you have is a deck of cards and someone knows the rules, but I can't imagine choosing to play this with all the variety of games that are now available!

[Rating: 3/10] No reason to play this (basic Whist) these days. It's difficult to think of many trick-takers which are worse than Whist. The strategy is extremely basic and there is not very much you can do to work around the deal.

[Rating: 4/10] About as bare-bones as you can get for a trick-taking game.  Since there's no card-pass after the deal, and you can't "go for control" or "shoot the moon," a bad hand is just a bad hand.  Can be fun played as a Court Whist tournament, though.

[Rating: 4/10] I was recently introduced to Whist, and upon playing discovered that I knew a lot of elements of the game from play in my youth without knowing I was doing Whist or a variant thereof. The versions I played involved getting an ever larger number of cards and playing with and without trump; and a version in which the full suit of cards is used, but requires the use of 2 bidding rounds. Whist in all its incarnations is a fairly simple cardgame without much hassle, nor requiring much strategic thought, although you can employ a few nice tactics. [Rating: 4/10] Boring.  There's about a million different games called whist, but every one is a trick-taking game, and I don't care much for trick-taking games.  The variant with which I am most familiar with is bid whist.  I'd rather play something more complicated in the same family, like Wizard, 500, or even Bridge.  This is one example where purity and simplicity really hurt the game and make it much more boring.

[Rating: 4/10] In Hawaii, there is a family of popular card games called "trumps", which are all variants of bid whist. When my family plays cards, this is almost always the game they play.
